Fixing bf16 pointer linkage for paged attention
Memory summary

This unit fixed an extension-loading failure in the first custom paged-attention kernel. The launch wrapper had requested data_ptr<__nv_bfloat16>(), which produced an undefined symbol at import time. It was changed to obtain untyped pointers and cast them to the kernel’s expected types. After slow shell and compilation attempts, check.py returned PASS. No benchmark score was produced in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The run had confirmed the target was an NVIDIA B200 with compute capability 10.0 and 148 SMs. The agent had written a single-query decode kernel using online softmax, shared-memory K/V staging, and one warp per query head within each GQA group. Its first correctness check failed before kernel execution: loading the extension raised an undefined-symbol error for TensorBase::data_ptr<__nv_bfloat16>().

Important non-obvious context
  • The trace reports capability 10.0 and CUDA 13.1; the extension compiled for sm_100a.
  • The kernel uses CUDA’s __nv_bfloat16, while the extension wrapper’s typed data_ptr<__nv_bfloat16>() lookup was not resolving. The fix preserved the kernel’s pointer types while obtaining pointers through PyTorch’s untyped accessor.
  • Shell commands were unusually slow: even a simple echo "hello" && date remained in the background before eventually completing. The trace timestamps are synthetic, so they do not establish actual elapsed time.
  • The reported correctness result is PASS; the unit has no benchmark score.
Recording summary

1. The agent traced the extension import error to data_ptr<__nv_bfloat16>() and updated the C++ launch wrapper. The central change was to cast pointers returned by untyped accessors:

``cpp auto* q_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat16*>(query.const_data_ptr()); auto* kv_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat16*>(kv_cache.const_data_ptr()); auto* bt_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const int32_t*>(block_table.const_data_ptr()); auto* sl_ptr = reinterpret_cast<const int32_t*>(seq_lens.const_data_ptr()); auto* out_ptr = reinterpret_cast<__nv_bfloat16*>(output.data_ptr()); ``

The kernel launch sites were changed to receive these local pointers instead of calling typed data_ptr at each launch.

2. The agent reran uv run python check.py 2>&1. The check remained in the background and produced no visible output during repeated polls. The agent inspected running processes, stopped the lingering check, and tried checking nvcc; that command also appeared stuck. A simple shell command eventually completed, confirming the shell was responsive but very slow.

3. The agent found an existing paged_attention_decode entry in the PyTorch extension cache and removed that cached build before retrying, to ensure the changed wrapper would be compiled.

4. The correctness rerun used a longer timeout:

``text command: uv run python check.py 2>&1 timeout: 600000 ``

The environment returned:

``text PASS ``

Split-K paged attention exposed a partial-buffer indexing bug

Split-K paged attention exposed a partial-buffer indexing bug
Memory summary

The agent responded to a low benchmark score by replacing the single-block-per-batch/KV-head kernel with a two-stage split-K design. It chose 256-token chunks, wrote per-chunk softmax partials, and added a merge kernel. The first correctness check failed on shape 0, seed 42: 6,290 of 32,768 values exceeded tolerance. The partial-buffer index mixed chunk, batch, and KV-head strides, causing the chunks’ partial results to overlap.

Relevant prior context

The original kernel had passed correctness across all five shapes and three seeds. Its benchmark achieved a geometric mean peak_fraction of 0.0283, below the agent’s stated 0.1 target. The grid (batch, num_kv_heads) produced only 32–64 blocks for several shapes, too few to occupy the B200’s 148 SMs. Shape 2, for example, reached 1.34% of peak bandwidth.

Important non-obvious context

The target GPU was an NVIDIA B200, capability 10.0, with CUDA 13.1. The task streams the KV cache, so the agent treated the low block count as an occupancy and memory-latency problem. The check output for this unit reports atol=0.05, rtol=0.05 for its large_q_kv case.

The new design used one chunk block per (chunk, batch, KV head). Within a block, each warp handled one query head in the GQA group, and K/V pages were staged in shared memory for reuse. A second kernel merged each head’s chunk results using the online-softmax (acc_o, m, l) formula.

Recording summary

The agent diagnosed the initial score as a parallelism problem and selected split-K. It set CHUNK_SIZE = 256 tokens (16 pages), planned a chunk kernel plus a reduction kernel, and rewrote solution.py. The chunk kernel stored float32 partial outputs and softmax statistics; the reduction kernel combined them and wrote bf16 output.

The indexing in the written code used:

int flat_idx = chunk_idx * partial_batch_stride
             + batch_idx * partial_kv_stride
             + kv_head * GROUP_SIZE
             + warp_id;

The host set partial_batch_stride = num_kv_heads * group_size and partial_kv_stride = group_size. This formula does not give each (batch, kv_head, chunk) its own disjoint region: the chunk term advances by only one batch’s head count, while batch and KV-head contributions are also combined in the same flat index. As a result, partials can overwrite one another before the reduce kernel reads them. A safe layout should derive one consistent flattened index—for example, (((batch * num_kv_heads + kv_head) * num_chunks_per_seq + chunk) * group_size + group_lane)—and use it identically in allocation, chunk writes, and reduction reads.

The check failed immediately on the first reported case:

Exit code 1
FAIL: shape 0 {'batch': 8, 'num_heads': 32, 'num_kv_heads': 8, 'head_dim': 128, 'seq_len': 1024, 'page_size': 16} seed 42 case large_q_kv: tolerance exceeded: max_abs_diff=0.188965 max_rel_diff=10880.5 bad=6290/32768 worst_idx=(5, 4, 123) (atol=0.05, rtol=0.05)

The official score remained 0.0283 through this unit; no new benchmark was run. Correctness changed from PASS before the unit to FAIL by its end. The next unit fixed the partial indexing and passed the check.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept_modified. The final solution retains the split-K chunk kernel and partial-result reduction introduced here, while using the corrected partial-buffer layout from unit 6.
  • Contribution: The first split-K version failed correctness and did not change the 0.0283 best score; its architecture nevertheless became the basis of the final kernel, which scored 0.063 officially.
  • Audit: none (the catalog and manifest mark the run unaudited, with no recorded audit finding).
  • Takeaway: Splitting KV work into chunks became the final parallelization strategy, but the original partial offsets collided and corrupted results. The idea held up only after unit 6 fixed the indexing.
Fixing split-K partial indexing in paged attention

Fixing split-K partial indexing in paged attention
Memory summary

This unit fixed the correctness regression introduced by split-K. The chunk kernel had used a batch stride that omitted the number of KV heads, so different (batch, kv_head) pairs could write to the same partial-buffer locations. The agent changed the layout to index partials by (chunk, batch, kv_head, head_in_group), cleared the extension cache, and got a passing correctness check. The best benchmark score remained 0.0283.

Relevant prior context

The original kernel passed correctness but achieved only 0.0283 peak fraction. Its grid exposed just 32–64 blocks for several shapes on a 148-SM B200, so the agent implemented split-K with 256-token chunks and a second kernel to merge partial online-softmax results.

The first split-K check failed on shape 0, seed 42, case large_q_kv. The run reported max_abs_diff=0.188965, max_rel_diff=10880.5, and 6290/32768 bad values. At the start of this unit, the agent was investigating page traversal, shared-memory sizing, and partial reduction indexing.

Important non-obvious context
  • The trace identifies the GPU as an NVIDIA B200, compute capability 10.0, with 148 SMs. The toolchain reports capability 10.0 and CUDA 13.1.
  • The corrected partial layout is (chunk, batch, kv_head, head_in_group), flattened as ((c * B + b) * Hkv + hkv) * G + g. This matches the Python partial tensors shaped (num_chunks * B * Hkv, G, head_dim).
  • The chunk kernel stages one page at a time. For HEAD_DIM=128 and PAGE_SIZE=16, sizing shared memory for one page uses 8 KB for K and V combined, instead of 128 KB when sized for a 256-token chunk.
  • The check exercised the large_q_kv stress case; its failure output reports atol=0.05, rtol=0.05. The task brief states a tolerance of 0.02.
  • This unit used 2 tool calls across 9 events. It made no benchmark measurement; the best score stayed at 0.0283.
Recording summary

The agent first reconsidered the failed output’s possible causes, including page boundaries and shared-memory use, then found that the old partial offset used batch_idx * GROUP_SIZE. Since the KV-head offset also used kv_head * GROUP_SIZE, adjacent batch/KV-head combinations could collide.

The rewritten kernel documents and uses a consistent partial layout:

// partials[chunk][batch][kv_head][head_in_group]
int flat_idx = ((c * B + b) * Hkv + hkv) * GROUP_SIZE + g;

The reduce kernel computes the same offset for each chunk before combining its (o, m, l) values. Python passes the partial buffers reshaped to match that flattened layout. The agent also changed the shared-memory arrays to PAGE_SIZE * HEAD_DIM, since only one page is staged at a time.

After the rewrite, the agent removed the cached extension and reran check.py. The environment returned:

PASS
Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: kept. The final solution indexes partials as chunk, batch, KV head, and group lane, matching the layout documented in this unit.
  • Contribution: It restored correctness for the split-K kernel; the best in-trace score stayed at 0.0283, while the eventual official run using this design scored 0.063.
  • Audit: none (the catalog and manifest mark the run unaudited, with no recorded audit finding).
  • Takeaway: The corrected indexing held up in the final solution and the official run passed correctness. Reducing shared memory to one page also remained part of the chunk kernel.

Paged-attention decode on B200: official score 0.063

Paged-attention decode on B200: official score 0.063
Memory summary

The final solution is a custom C++/CUDA extension in solution.py. Each chunk kernel processes 256 tokens for one batch and KV head, with one warp per query head in its GQA group. It streams paged K/V data through shared memory, accumulates online-softmax partials, and a second kernel combines those partials into bf16 output. The official run passed correctness and scored 0.063 peak bandwidth fraction on B200.

Relevant prior context

The first correctness attempt failed while loading the extension with an undefined bfloat16 data_ptr symbol. The agent changed pointer handling, after which the check passed. The initial benchmark scored 0.0283 and was reported LOW, prompting a split-K redesign.

The first split-K correctness run exposed incorrect partial-buffer indexing. The agent corrected the flat index to represent (chunk, batch, kv_head, head_in_group) and reran the check successfully. The in-trace benchmark then exited with code 137 before reporting results; the later official rundetail records a completed benchmark and a higher final score of 0.063.

Important non-obvious context
  • The workload is memory-bound. The benchmark computes each shape’s peak fraction from achieved DRAM bandwidth divided by the B200’s stated 8,000 GB/s peak, then aggregates fractions with a geometric mean.
  • The five tested shapes were (8,32,8,128,1024,16), (32,32,8,128,2048,16), (4,64,8,128,4096,16), (16,32,8,128,1535,16), and (8,16,4,64,2000,16).
  • The official check covers all five shapes, three seeds, numeric stress cases, and a property-stress check. The rundetail records correct: true; the run summary records correctness PASS.
  • The solution uses host-side sequence-length inspection (seq_lens.max().item() and a CPU copy in the extension) to determine chunk count. It also makes inputs contiguous in forward, which can add overhead when inputs are not already contiguous.
  • The leaderboard calculation places the run 11th among 12 scored entries out of 14 cells; the best listed score was 0.2639. The catalog and manifest both mark the run unaudited, so the passing result has no recorded audit verdict.

Recording summary

The final kernel uses CHUNK_SIZE = 256, a multiple of the 16-token page size. For each chunk, a CTA handles one (batch, kv_head) pair; each warp handles one query head in that KV head’s GQA group. It loads one page of K and V into shared memory, computes Q·K scores with warp reductions, and updates (acc_o, m, l) online-softmax state. A reduction kernel merges chunk partials using the online-softmax combine rule and writes bf16 output.
